environment.what_these_numbers_are: Definitions, exports, import edges and supertypes are exact set comparisons against hand-authored truth, inherited from spike s1 and extended for the two relations only a shipped extractor needs. They are a statement about THIS extractor, not about the grammars: s1's report is the grammar measurement, this is the implementation's.

cases.sentence: structure unavailable: not one of the grammars fathom reads
structure unavailable: the parse reported 3 errors and returned no structure
structure unavailable: the file is not text
structure unavailable: the file is larger than the 13 byte extraction limit

fallback.mean: AC 2: an unknown or broken language yields structure unavailable plus file-level analysis, never a lost episode. `broken.rs` may parse — tree-sitter recovers — and that is the honest outcome, so it is reported rather than asserted.

never_lost.mean: AC 2: every file comes back, with a reason when there is no structure. `unavailable` here is 0 for a clean corpus; the `fallback` battery below is what proves the non-zero path works.

forced_one_pass.mean: the same corpus, re-extracted with `extract.resolution.max_passes = 1`. One pass is not enough to *observe* stability for any file that resolved something — a fixpoint is proved by a pass that changes nothing — so the honest report names those files instead of calling them settled. A file with nothing to resolve converged on the spot and is not listed.

resolution.mean: s1 finding 6: resolution is iterative, so it is bounded per file and the bound is a config key. `non_converged` names the files where the bound bit; on this corpus it is empty by construction, and `--max-passes 1` makes it non-empty on purpose.

synthetic_eligible.mean: s1 finding 1: a scope a program wrote into is a scope that cannot be enumerated. `missing` is the number that matters; a marked scope never yields a 'declares nothing' assertion, which is what `scopes_that_assert_emptiness` proves.

wildcard_edges.mean: s1 finding 2: a star import is a real dependency of unknown contents. `who_depends_on` is the AC made visible — the answer must name the unknown files, never say nobody.

throughput_check.mean: the replica, measured: files per second per core is the contract because ADR-004's budgets are paid per changed file; MiB/s is reported next to spike s1's parse-only figure to show what resolution adds on top of parsing. A debug build exempts both, because a debug build measures the borrow checker.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per `impl <trait> for <type>` and per `trait X: Y`, kind `trait`, because a Rust `impl` is a contract fulfilment and not an ancestry; `impl Point` (inherent) is deliberately absent, because an inherent impl adds members and changes no relationship. `impl fmt::Debug for Shape` names the base as written (`Debug`), not as resolved, because `e3.2` draws the edge and needs the name the reader will look for.
languages.truth_notes: The corpus is a crate root: `lib.rs` declares the module tree, so module paths are derivable. Hand-annotated against the Rust reference, not against any parser. Definitions are what a file *declares*, cfg-gated arms included (a file that declares both arms declares two definitions). Export is the crate's external surface: an item is exported if a file outside this crate could name it in a *default unix build* — which needs the item's own visibility (`pub`, not `pub(crate)`), every module on its path from the crate root being `pub`, and, for an item in a private module, a public re-export somewhere that gives it a public path. That is the reading `e3.7`'s public-API surface needs, and it is the one that makes `pub use` load-bearing: `secret::helper` is public only because `lib.rs` re-exports it. Members are excluded from the export set (top level only). Associated items of an impl for an external type are attributed to the self type's base name (`Vec.measured`), because that is what a graph node for 'method of Vec declared in this file' means.
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: `macros.rs` only. The file declares two `macro_rules!` and invokes both at file scope, so items exist that no token stream contains, and the honest scope is the file — a macro arm is not confined to the item it writes. No other file in this corpus earns the mark: `cfg` arms are text, `#[derive]` is an attribute the extractor can name, and marking a cfg-gated module synthetic would throw away two real definitions to describe a build-time choice.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per `class X(Y)`. `NamedTuple` and `TypedDict` are recorded as bases because the corpus classes genuinely declare them, and because the consequence — the members come from the base, not the file — is exactly what the row is for; `resolved` stays absent for them since they live outside the corpus. Python's keyword form `class X(metaclass=M)` would be kind `metaclass`; this corpus has none, and saying so is better than inventing one.
languages.truth_notes: The corpus root is a package, so `from .models import Shape` is a relative import with a determinate target. Export is `__all__` where a module defines one, otherwise every module-level name without a leading underscore — a rule about names, not about declarations, so a re-export (`from .models import Shape` in `__init__.py`) is a definition the file does not have and an export it does not own; those land in the import relation instead. `@dataclass` writes an `__init__`, so a decorated class's generated `__init__` is annotated as a definition: the decorator is documented to do it, and whether a parser knows that is the measured question, not a thing the annotation gets to skip. A module-level binding assigned a `namedtuple(...)` call is a class. Statements inside a function body are not symbols, but imports inside a function body *are* import edges, because Python's lazy imports are load-bearing for the dependency graph.
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: `dynamic.py` and `models.py`. dynamic.py: a module-level `__getattr__` and a `globals()[...]` write put names in the module no file declares (`dynamic_method`), and `Shape.describe = lambda ...`, `Slate.extra = property(...)` write members into classes from the outside (`monkeypatch`); `Box`/`Movie` are a `NamedTuple` and a `TypedDict`, so their members are added by the base (`synthesised_accessors`); `Slate` carries a decorator that replaces the class (`decorated`). models.py: both dataclasses have members `@dataclass` writes (`decorated`, and `synthesised_accessors` because the decorator is known to add `__init__`/`__eq__`/`__repr__`). registry.py is deliberately NOT marked: `@register` writes a dispatch table, not members of a scope, and pretending otherwise would mark half of every Flask application unenumerable — the honest record of it is the `decorated_by:register` modifier, and the category is in `thresholds.json` under `irreducible_blind_spots.python` as `runtime_registration`.

languages.truth_bases_notes: One row per `implements` and per `extends`. `implements Shape` is kind `interface` and `extends Base` is kind `base`, because the two answer different questions — `who fulfils this contract` and `who inherits this state` — and a pane that merges them cannot tell a refactor from a subtype change. This corpus has no `extends` row, which is a gap in the corpus, not a claim about TypeScript.
languages.truth_notes: ES modules. An import of a name re-exported by a barrel resolves to the *origin* file (the barrel is a hop, recorded on the importing file as one edge with `barrel_hop`); a barrel's own export set is empty because it declares nothing. A default export is the exported name `default`, and the local name is an alias. Two `export interface Config` blocks in one file are declaration merging: one symbol, two declaration sites. A module-level binding whose initialiser is a function value is a `fn`, not a `var`. Members are excluded from the export set.
languages.truth_synthetic_notes: index.ts and geo/index.ts are barrels: `export * from './shapes'` means the module's export list is whatever the target exports, which no read of the barrel can enumerate (`wildcard_reexport`). types.d.ts is ambient: an `.d.ts` describes declarations that may be merged by any other `.d.ts` in the program (`ambient_merge`). legacy.ts earns `ambient_merge` for two reasons at once: two `export interface Config` blocks that TypeScript merges into one declaration, and a `declare module 'virtual:thing'` block whose contents a bundler writes into a module that has no file. consumer.ts is NOT marked: it imports names, which is a claim the file can make.

granularity.definitions: one row per named declaration at file top level or inside a type/module container, members included, function-local declarations excluded; a cfg-gated or conditional arm that declares a second copy of a name is the same row, because the graph is a set of names, not a count of tokens
granularity.exports: one row per top-level symbol nameable from outside the declaring unit, per the language's own access rules
granularity.imports: one row per (file, resolved corpus file, symbol) dependency, with symbol `*` for a dependency whose contents the file does not name
granularity.supertypes: one row per (file, declaring symbol, base as written), kind `base`, `trait`, `interface` or `metaclass`
granularity.synthetic: one row per (file, dotted scope) that cannot be enumerated from the file, with the reason words the extractor uses

thresholds.how_thresholds_are_set: Recall is the bar that matters for a graph, because a missing edge is an invisible dependency and an invisible dependency is the failure ADR-004's whole argument is about. Precision matters more for an export surface, because a wrong `public` is a false promise in a breaking-change report. Each floor is stated as (a) what a reviewer would notice and (b) what a grammar plus a language model can actually deliver, and `hard: true` means 'missing this makes the language unusable for `e3.2`..`e3.7` at file granularity, so it goes to the fallback rather than to a caveat'. The numbers are spike `s1`'s, deliberately: the spike measured what these grammars deliver, and re-measuring its own guess is not how this ticket should move the bar.

irreducible_blind_spots.what: Categories the extractor cannot remove at any effort level, per language, because the information is not in the file. A run that records one of these still passes, but the verdict is `conditions`: the category is stated as a limitation rather than rounded away. Anything the corpus shows that is not listed here is a bug in the extractor, not a property of the language.

irreducible_tags.what: The annotation tags whose *definition rows* are removed from the scored set, because the declaration is not textually in the file at all: a `macro_rules!` arm, a `@dataclass`-written `__init__`, a monkeypatched method, a webpack virtual module. This is not leniency wearing a hat — the alternative is scoring the extractor against rows no file-granularity parser can produce, which teaches it to guess. What the extractor owes instead is the honest state, and `mechanisms.synthetic_eligible` is where that debt is collected: the scope the row lives in must come back marked.

mechanisms.never_lost: Every input file returns a record. A file with no structure returns a reason and its file-level measurement. Losing a file is the failure mode that turns a wrong number into an invisible one.
mechanisms.resolution: Resolution is a bounded iteration, and the bound is a config key, and the report says how many passes were used and whether the file converged. Non-convergence is a bug to fix, not a caveat; `--max-passes 1` exists so the bound can be shown to bite rather than asserted.
mechanisms.synthetic_eligible: Every scope the corpus marks must come back marked. A marked scope must never produce a 'declares nothing' assertion: the surface may say 'may have shrunk, not shrunk', and nothing stronger. Missing a scope is a fail, not a condition, because an unmarked dynamic scope is a confidently wrong answer about code that changed.
mechanisms.what: The four checks in the report's `mechanisms` block, and what each one costs when it fails. These are not extra accuracy metrics — they are the four ways a clean set score can still describe a useless extractor, which is the argument spike `s1` spent its planning budget making.
mechanisms.wildcard_edges: Every `*` import in the corpus must arrive as its own edge kind, and `dependents_of` must answer 'who depends on X' by naming the wildcard files as *unknown-content dependents*. Reporting a star import as a resolved named edge, or answering 'nobody', is a fail: both are the same lie told twice.

definitions.mean: A definition is one named declaration at file top level or inside a type/module container, members included, function-local declarations excluded. Missing 5 % of them means 5 % of the code has no node in the graph, and a file with no node cannot be reviewed.

exports.mean: One row per top-level symbol nameable from outside the declaring unit, per the language's own access rules — Rust's re-export rule, Python's `__all__`-or-underscore rule, TypeScript's `export`-plus-barrel rule. Precision is the higher bar here: a false `public` is a wrong breaking-change report, which is worse than a missing one.

imports.mean: One row per (file, resolved corpus file, symbol) dependency, wildcard rows included with symbol `*`. Ten percent is the price of dynamic module systems — a Python `importlib.import_module` and a TypeScript namespace import are genuinely unresolvable at file granularity.

supertypes.mean: One row per declared base, implemented trait or implemented interface. Recall is the higher bar: `who implements Shape?` is the question the architecture pane draws, and a missing `impl` is a hole in the shape of the system.

throughput.comment: Parse-plus-extract throughput per core, release profile, measured on a deterministic 4 000-file replica of the corpus because 9 fixture files measure process startup. ADR-004's `cold.graph.ms` and `warm.graph.marginal.ms` are paid per changed file, so files-per-second-per-core is the contract and 1 000 files/s clears a 5 000-file warm pass by three orders of magnitude. The MiB/s figure is a canary, stated second because source files are small and uneven: spike `s1` measured 5 MiB/s parse-only, and this number is parse *plus* resolution, whose cost grows with the corpus rather than the file. Both floors are enforced in a release build and exempt in a debug build, which measures bounds checks rather than the extractor. Missing a floor is a condition, never a no-go: cost is a feature-gate question (ADR-002 §6.5).

thresholds.verdict_rule: pass: every relation at or above its floor, and no mechanism missed, and the throughput floor met in a release build. conditions: every `hard` floor met, but a soft floor missed, a row missed or found that the floors tolerate, or an irreducible blind spot recorded. fail: a `hard` floor missed, or any mechanism check missed — a mechanism is not a quality bar, it is the definition of what the output is allowed to claim.
thresholds.what: The acceptance bar for `e3.1` (`reco-zoz`): the structural extractor core for Rust, Python and TypeScript, plus the four mechanisms spike `s1` handed over as non-negotiables. A language that misses a `hard` floor is not cut from the plan — it is stated as what this build does not do, in the report and in `docs/concepts/structure-extraction.md`, and the language's files come back with a reason instead of a silently thin graph.
